source.title: Safety alignment should be made more than just a few tokens deep
source.authors: Xiangyu Qi; Ashwinee Panda; Kaifeng Lyu; Xiao Ma; Subhrajit Roy; Ahmad Beirami; Prateek Mittal; Peter Henderson

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present. Some equations and figure content are flattened in the web text, but this does not prevent extracting the stated results.
record.tranche_reason: It repeats harmful and benign fine-tuning safety evaluations using the harmfulness-rate/ASR approach of the cited fine-tuning study, and also directly measures token-wise KL and tests prefilling and other attacks.
record.gate_note: The paper also discusses adversarial suffixes and other attacks from cited work; those cited results are not recorded. For its own GCG and decoding-parameter experiments, results are recorded below. Figure-only token-wise curves are recorded as figure-only where the text does not give their plotted values.
record.test_reason: It reruns the Qi et al. fine-tuning attacks and benign fine-tuning with the same GPT-4 judge and HEx-PHI harmfulness rate. It measures aligned-vs-base per-token KL and tests prefilling, GCG and decoding attacks. It also builds and tests a deepening augmentation. It is one of the claim's two original sources, so no verdict labels are given.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors argue current alignment mainly changes the first few output tokens, which unifies prefilling, suffix, decoding and fine-tuning vulnerabilities. They show that recovery-example augmentation deepens alignment and improves robustness to tested attacks. It remains vulnerable to harmful fine-tuning. A first-token-constrained fine-tuning objective mitigates fine-tuning attacks.
record.recipe_differences: Uses the cited harmful fine-tuning safety evaluation approach and harmfulness/ASR measure, while adding token-wise KL analyses, prefilling and inference-stage attack tests, safety-recovery augmentation, and a constrained fine-tuning objective.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary by model, fine-tuning dataset, attack type, prefill length, trigger presence, and whether standard or constrained SFT is used. The paper states that empty system prompts generally lead to higher ASR for prefilling and decoding-parameter attacks; GCG uses the official system prompt.

fits_no_version.finding: Harmful fine-tuning shifts the per-token KL from the initially aligned model most at early token positions (Fig. 3c). Per-token loss and gradient norms are also largest at early positions.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Fine-tuning attacks act mainly on the first few response tokens.

fits_no_version.finding: Constraining updates on the first 5 tokens keeps ASR low after harmful, identity-shifting, backdoor and benign fine-tuning with similar utility. Uniform small β fails; uniform large β collapses utility (Table 4).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Protecting initial-token distributions during fine-tuning preserves safety.

fits_no_version.finding: Prefilling refusal prefixes into base models cuts harmfulness from 68.6% and 85.4% to roughly 1–16% (Table 1).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A refusal prefix alone puts unaligned models into a safe mode.

record.problems: The authors could not access the original Llama-2 alignment data and pipeline, so augmentation was tested by further fine-tuning an already aligned model rather than training alignment from scratch. Some key token-wise results are figures without numerical values in the text. The reported attack results use limited model and dataset settings; GCG results are selected from the three most successful runs.
record.rows_left_out: The 60-row cap was reached. Left out Table 1's multiple refusal-prefix conditions on base and aligned models, which show that prefilled refusal prefixes reduce harmfulness in base models; additional Table 6 fine-tuning-method arms for augmented-model harmful and identity-shifting attacks; utility scores; and per-token loss/gradient-norm curves. The left-out safety-prefix results are in Section 2.2, Table 1; remaining augmented-model safety results are in Appendix C, Table 6.

untested.parts: Only 100-example harmful sets on two 7B models. The full few-to-few-hundred range and larger or closed models are not tested.
Only Samsum, SQL Create Context and GSM8k. No carefully selected benign data.
Only Llama-2-7B and Gemma-7B. Per-position values are figure-only.
Prefilling on two models; GCG and decoding exploit only on Llama-2-7B-Chat.
No weight or rank localization experiment.
Explanation is argued (SFT and RLHF data rarely contain recovery-after-harm text). Table 1 shows the refusal-prefix shortcut exists, but alignment data or objective are never varied.
Augmentation is applied as further fine-tuning of an already aligned model, not alignment from scratch. Only Llama-2-7B-Chat. No adaptive attacks.

missing.what: Gemma-7B-IT prefilling ASR curve versus number of prefilled harmful tokens (figure only)
Standard SFT with 10-step learning-rate warmup on the non-augmented model. Benign ASR drops to 3.8% (Samsum) and 3.3% (SQL) versus 23.4% and 15.4% without warmup. Identity shifting falls to 44.8%.
Utility cost of augmentation: AlpacaEval win rate 49.5% vs 51.8% for the initial model
Refusal prefixes Llama-2-7B-Chat uses in 96.1% of cases, and Gemma's "I am unable" in 96.7%

record.verdict_notes: This paper is one of the claim's listed original sources, so no verdict labels are given. Rows are relinked for when it serves as a reference point. For V1 and V2 it reproduces the other original (arXiv:2310.03693) on Llama-2-7B-Chat and adds Gemma-1.1-7B-IT, where benign fine-tuning barely raises ASR (2.0–2.9% vs 1.8%). Main record errors: identity-shifting baselines are 0±0, not 1.5 or 1.8. Augmented rows were double-linked to V4. Table 6 rows lacked the non-augmented comparator, and the benign-durability states were inverted. Constrained-SFT rows are the authors' own method, not V1 or V2 instances. GCG ASR is the mean of the 3 best of 10 runs. Prefilling and decoding attacks use an empty system prompt.

versions.untested_parts: The paper tests specified harmful fine-tuning datasets and configurations, not every training recipe or all counts from a few to a few hundred examples.
Tests the named downstream datasets and configurations; does not test all ordinary or carefully selected benign datasets.
The plotted per-position values are not stated numerically in the text.
Tests prefilling, GCG, and decoding-parameter attacks. It does not itself report a separate adversarial-suffix result, and does not test every decoding strategy.
No experiment localizes safety in a small set of weights or ranks.
The paper proposes explanations about alignment data and objectives, but does not experimentally vary the original safety-alignment data or objective to test what causes shallow alignment.
Deepening and robustness are tested for the paper's augmentation and evaluated attacks; the authors note that they did not train an alignment pipeline from scratch.

statements.correction: Table 3: Llama-2-7B-Chat 1.5±0.2%→88.9±1.2%; Gemma-1.1-7B-IT 1.8±0.3%→81.6±2.9%. Appendix A.2: ASR counts outputs receiving GPT-4-Turbo score 5; metric explicitly identified as identical to Qi et al.'s harmfulness rate.

statements.correction: Section 2.3.2: 100 harmful instruction–answer pairs; batch size 64; learning rate 2×10^-5. Figure 3: ASR 22.4%, 76.4%, and 87.9% after two, four, and six gradient steps. No matched joint sweep establishing minimum unique harmful pairs separately from exposure.
